Celebrating Academic Excellence Across A Level and GCSE Results at Cranleigh School
Cranleigh School is delighted to share another year of exceptional academic and co-curricular achievements. From impressive top-tier grades in STEM and the Humanities to outstanding performances in the Creative and Performing Arts, our Upper Sixth and Year 11 pupils have demonstrated remarkable dedication, balancing rigorous academic success with vibrant involvement in school life.
Discover the full stories and detailed breakdowns for each year group below.
Is Cranleigh School Right For My Child?
A place where every child can be themselves
At Cranleigh, we know and value every pupil for who they are. Our culture gives children the confidence to try new things, find their strengths, and grow into thoughtful, and resilient young people ready for the world.
Learning & Growth
Ambition for every child
We encourage pupils to aim high, ask questions and take real pride in their work. Supported by outstanding teachers who know them as individuals, children stay curious and build the confidence to chase their goals at School and in life beyond.
Bringing out the best
Strong academic results start with knowing each child, who they are and what drives them. When pupils feel supported and understood, they are ready to push themselves, take on challenges and achieve results they can be truly proud of. See below our academic results for 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions
Helping You Find Answers
Choosing a school is a big decision for any family. Here are clear answers to the questions parents ask us most often about life at Cranleigh.
What age do pupils join Cranleigh School?
Pupils can join Cranleigh from age 3 to 18. Our main entry points are Pre-School (age 3), Reception (age 4), Year 7 (age 11), Year 9 (age 13) and Sixth Form (age 16). We also welcome pupils into other year groups whenever space is available.
Is Cranleigh School co-educational?
Yes. Cranleigh is a co-educational independent school for pupils aged 3 to 18, bringing our Prep and Senior Schools together across two neighbouring sites. Boys and girls learn, work and grow up alongside one another in a warm, grounded environment.
Is Cranleigh a boarding or day school?
At Cranleigh Senior, we offer flexible choices to suit family life, including Day, Day Plus (our flexible boarding option), Weekly Boarding and Full Boarding. Whichever path you choose, every pupil enjoys the same strong sense of belonging and excellent personal care.
At Cranlegh Prep, pupils can board from Year 3 onwards, most typically they start from Year 5. They can board on an ad hoc, flexi, or full basis.
What are Cranleigh’s fees?
Fees depend on your child’s age and whether they attend as a day pupil or boarder. It will also depend on whether they take part in specialist teaching, clubs and activities outside the wide range of activities already available to them. You can find full details on our fees page.
Details on our Pre-Prep and Pre-School fees can be found here.
Details on our Prep fees can be found here.
Details on our Senior fees can be found here.
Does Cranleigh offer scholarships and bursaries?
Yes. We offer scholarships to recognise talent, achievement or potential in academics, sport, music, drama, design engineering and art. We also offer bursaries (financial support based on family income) to help families with fees. You can find out more about this on our Admissions page.

What drama is available at Cranleigh Senior?
Drama at our independent school in Surrey is a vibrant part of school life, giving students the opportunity to perform, create and develop their confidence both on and off stage. With industry-grade facilities, two dedicated drama studios and experienced staff, pupils are encouraged to take creative risks, find their voice and discover their potential as performers and theatre-makers.
Cranleigh Senior drama productions run throughout the year, offering opportunities for pupils to act, direct, design and contribute behind the scenes. From House Drama and year-group performances to major musicals and student-led productions, students develop their skills as part of a creative community where collaboration, imagination and ambition thrive.
How does Cranleigh nurture future performers?
Cranleigh Senior drama students follow a five-year artistic pathway from ages 13 to 18, designed to nurture talent, build confidence and prepare students for future study and careers in the performing arts.
Through practical experience, expert teaching and industry insight, pupils develop their craft both in the classroom and through ambitious productions. They benefit from direct connections with the professional theatre world through workshops, masterclasses and one-to-one training with actors, directors and designers, while opportunities to perform in professional theatre venues provide valuable experience of larger-scale productions.
Led by Director of Performing Arts Stephen Whitson, an experienced West End director, the department gives pupils insight into the standards and expectations of the professional industry. Backstage and technical roles are valued equally alongside performance, with students gaining hands-on experience in technical theatre, production management and the skills required to run full-scale productions.
Cranleigh’s strong performing arts pathway has supported pupils in progressing to leading drama schools in the UK and USA, with alumni going on to pursue successful careers across the creative industries.
What drama events are coming up at Cranleigh Senior?
The stage is alive with productions and showcases throughout the year. Students take part in major school productions, House Drama, year-group shows and the Performing Arts Festival — a celebration of Music, Drama and Dance featuring student and staff-led performances on a full size festival stage.
Pupils also have the opportunity to collaborate with performers across Cranleigh’s wider international school community, creating shared experiences, exchanging culture and celebrating creativity on a global stage.

What music opportunities are available at Senior?
Music is an important part of Senior life. Pupils develop as performers, listeners, creators and thinkers, combining academic study with practical creativity and collaborative performance. From classroom lessons to concerts and twice a week Chapel singing – supported by the school’s Mander Organ, one of the best in the country – music shapes the rhythm of the school day. Whether performing, composing or simply enjoying being part of the audience, every pupil is encouraged to engage with music in a way that feels good to them.
What music events happen at Cranleigh Senior?
Music is active and visible across our independent school in Surrey, with a full calendar of concerts, productions and Chapel performances happening throughout the year.
Cranleigh pupils regularly take part in:
The school also hosts a concert series with professional performers across many genres, with a particular focus on diversity and underrepresented voices. International collaborations, including exchanges with Cranleigh Abu Dhabi, add richness to the programme.

Orchestra and ensemble performances

How does music tuition work at Cranleigh Senior?
How does music tuition work at Cranleigh Senior?
Music tuition at Cranleigh Senior combines academic study with extensive practical opportunities, giving pupils a rich and well-rounded music education.
Cranleigh Senior music opportunities include:
Music is treated as an intellectual, creative and collaborative discipline. Pupils develop technical skills alongside listening, analysis and creative thinking, while exploring a wide range of musical styles.

What professional musicians visit Cranleigh?
What professional musicians visit Cranleigh?
Alongside Cranleigh’s own teaching staff – all professional musicians – the school regularly welcomes visiting artists who bring real-world experience into school life.
Recent collaborators include Korros Ensemble, the Band of the Coldstream Guards, Amelie Jat (singer-songwriter), Orpheus Sinfonia and Zeb Soanes (Classic FM). A strong focus on diversity and cultural exchange, including a partnership with Black Lives in Music, ensures pupils engage with a wide range of musical styles and traditions.
Cranleigh has also developed many musicians who go on to achieve success, including international conductor Sarah Ioannides and singer Hilary Cronin.

Frequently asked questions – Senior music
Who leads the Senior Music department?
Mr Richard Saxel has been Director of Music since September 2019, but has taught Music at Cranleigh since 2001, previously as Head of Performance. He combines teaching at Cranleigh School with a successful career as an international concert pianist, and has performed, recorded and broadcast around the world to critical acclaim, and with a wide variety of musicians. He studied Music with History of Art at the University of York and Piano Accompaniment at the Royal Academy of Music, which awarded him Associateship in recognition of his significant contribution to the music profession.
What makes music at Cranleigh special?
Music at Cranleigh combines academic rigour with creativity and performance. Pupils work with professional musicians, explore a wide range of styles, and take part in a rich programme of concerts, collaborations and cultural exchange.
What is the cost of music tuition?
Music tuition is charged per term, per instrument, with fees detailed in a published schedule found in our application form.
Is music a part of everyday life?
Yes. Music is woven into daily life at Cranleigh, particularly through regular Chapel singing and a full programme of performances and events.
Can pupils join a choir or orchestra?
Yes. Pupils usually join a choir or orchestra by audition or invitation. Ensembles are available at different levels to support both confident performers and those developing their skills.
Are there overseas tours?
Yes. Choirs and orchestras tour internationally, giving pupils opportunities to perform in new settings, collaborate with other musicians and experience different musical cultures.
Can pupils take music exams?
Yes, pupils can prepare for and take ABRSM (Associated Board of the Royal Schools of Music) and Trinity exams as part of their musical development.

What is the Cranleigh Advanced Diploma?
The Cranleigh Year 12 & 13 Diploma (Advanced) builds on everything pupils learn in the Foundation and Intermediate Diplomas. It is delivered through our Futures Programme and a curriculum shaped by our core values – Aspire Boldly, Be Yourself and Care for Others – helping pupils grow the confidence and practical experience they need for university, apprenticeships and professional life.
How does the Year 12 & 13 Diploma help every child reach their potential?
The Advanced Diploma helps every pupil develop the key skills that matter most. Pupils strengthen these skills through STRIDE, which stands for Stewardship, Technology, Readiness, Innovation, Diversity and Economic literacy. This unique curriculum helps pupils at our independent school in Surrey build the independence, self-awareness and real-world readiness they need to thrive beyond Sixth Form.

What do Cranleigh Year 12 & 13 Diploma pupils study?
Pupils take part in two weekly STRIDE lessons, providing lively, hands-on opportunities to grow their confidence, curiosity and practical skills for school and beyond. Alongside their academic studies, pupils can dive into activities such as academic reading, join debating societies, take on innovation challenges such as Vex Robotics or sustainability projects such as Green Dragons, where teams pitch environmentally focused business ideas to a panel of “dragons”. It’s a broad, exciting mix that encourages pupils to stretch their interests and try something new.
This balance of classroom learning and real-world opportunities helps pupils develop the skills and character to thrive beyond the classroom – and is what we call the Cranleigh Difference. Through this we enable pupils to unlock their passions and create opportunities for them.

No - it’s designed to work alongside A Level study.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our approach to AI | Cranleigh School
pageCache.text:
Saturday 12th September - 08:45 to 11:30.
How does Cranleigh prepare pupils for a world shaped by AI?
AI is changing how people work, create and access information, and our role is to help pupils develop the judgement, curiosity and critical thinking they need to use it wisely. Cranleigh's approach to AI is rooted in our core values – Aspire Boldly, Be Yourself and Care for Others – and these values shape everything that follows.
We encourage pupils to explore new technologies with ambition, to use them in ways that support creativity and authentic expression, and to understand the ethical and environmental implications of AI. Above all, we want pupils to leave Cranleigh confident in navigating a world shaped by technology while still thinking independently, communicating clearly and staying true to themselves.
How do we use AI in education?
At our independent school in Surrey, AI follows the same approach we apply to all digital use. It’s used carefully and only when it genuinely supports learning and good thinking. When pupils use AI, it’s framed openly and linked to Cranleigh’s CHAT principles – encouraging critical questioning, prioritising human judgement, keeping learning authentic and being transparent about how AI was used. AI can support ideas and thinking, but it never replaces them.
AI, and the use of it, is also taught through our STRIDE curriculum delivered through our diplomas - with Sixth Form pupils feeling employment ready to work alongside AI when they leave Cranleigh.
How will my child know what AI use is allowed?
Cranleigh makes it clear when AI can be used through a traffic light system applied per assessment, per task, per subject. This ensures pupils always know what is permitted, what must be cited, and when independent work is required.
AI guidance also sits alongside wider digital wellbeing, safeguarding and learning policies so pupils grow into ethical, balanced and future-ready users of technology.
AI traffic light system
Level 0 – No AI. Pupils complete all parts of the task themselves: planning, ideas, research, drafting and final work. Examples: in-class essays, prep tasks, traditional exams, early-stage brainstorming.
Level 1 – AI for ideas and structure. AI can help with initial thinking or outlining, but pupils must develop and shape the work themselves. Examples: brainstorming arguments, sketching a research outline and exploring possible structures.
Level 2 – AI for polishing and checking. The core thinking and analysis must be the pupil’s own. Examples: proofreading, checking dates, finding an extra example after pupils have provided their own.
Level 3 – AI for creative use. AI can be used throughout the task, including generating content, as long as pupils curate, refine and show critical understanding of the output. Examples: AI-generated stories or poems, presentations with AI-created visuals, scenario simulations in subjects like economics or computer science.
Preparing pupils for the future
Beyond classroom teaching, pupils have opportunities to explore AI through project-based learning, innovation and leadership experiences. Specialist pathways, qualifications and enrichment activities allow older pupils to engage with AI in increasingly sophisticated ways.
Cranleigh is also investing significantly in staff development, curriculum design and research-informed practice through the Cranleigh Centre for Research. Our work towards recognised AI quality standards reflects our commitment to leading – not simply following – developments in this field.
Our aim is neither to ban AI nor embrace it uncritically. Instead, we help pupils become thoughtful, capable and ethical users of powerful new technologies: young people who can aspire boldly, be themselves and care for others in a world shaped by AI.

How does the Cranleigh AI traffic light system work?
The Cranleigh AI traffic-light system offers pupils clear guidance on when and how they can use AI in their work. Green tasks allow pupils to use helpful tools to brainstorm, organise ideas or polish their writing. Amber tasks ask pupils to proceed carefully – they can use AI for limited support, but they must show their own thinking and judgement. Red tasks mean AI isn’t appropriate at all, usually because the work needs to be fully independent.
It’s a simple framework that helps pupils build digital confidence, practise responsible use and develop good judgement, while keeping learning rooted in real thinking and discussion.
